title: Conversation Mistakes You Don't Know You're MAKING
title_alternatives: Why People Stop LISTENING When You Talk
The Hidden Mistakes That Make Conversations AWKWARD
People Like You More Than You THINK
The Question That Makes People LIKE You
description:
You leave a conversation sure you sounded boring. Research says people probably liked you more than you think. Five everyday conversation mistakes, what the studies found, and the simple fix for each, including the one kind of question that makes people like you.

This video is psychology for education, not professional advice.

Sources:
- Boothby et al. (2018). The liking gap in conversations. Psychological Science.
- Tamir & Mitchell (2012). Disclosing information about the self is intrinsically rewarding. PNAS.
- Derber (1979/2000). The Pursuit of Attention.
- Newton (1990). Song-tapping study, Stanford; Heath & Heath, Made to Stick.
- Stivers et al. (2009). Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation. PNAS.
- Huang et al. (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. JPSP.
- Kardas, Kumar & Epley (2022). Overly shallow? JPSP.
- Mastroianni et al. (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS.

scenes.narration: You know that replay after a party?

scenes.narration: Did I talk too much? Was that joke weird?

scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: Here's the strange part.

scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: So the signals were there. We just missed them.

scenes.narration: Why do we miss them?

scenes.narration: One of the researchers said we're too wrapped up in our own worries.

scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: We're busy grading ourselves instead of watching them.

scenes.narration: That worry is behind almost every mistake that follows.

scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: Think about the last time you met someone new.

scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: They were too busy worrying about their own clumsy moments.

scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: Honestly? This one changed how I feel after parties.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character smiles and relaxes on a balcony at night, city lights below.

scenes.narration: The other person probably enjoyed it more than you think.
scenes.image_prompt: Two friends walking away from each other after a hug, both smiling, autumn street.
scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: Mistake one sounds friendly. It isn't.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits with a friend at lunch, mouth open, about to interrupt.

scenes.narration: People spend about a third of their talk on themselves.
scenes.image_prompt: A pie made of three slices on a white plate, one slice glowing gold.
scenes.fact_source: Tamir & Mitchell (2012). Disclosing information about the self is intrinsically rewarding. PNAS 109, 8038-8043

scenes.narration: And it isn't just ego.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character shrugs with an innocent grin, holding a coffee cup.

scenes.image_prompt: A glowing brain scan image on a lab monitor in a dark room, warm colours in the center.
scenes.fact_source: Tamir & Mitchell (2012). Disclosing information about the self is intrinsically rewarding. PNAS 109, 8038-8043

scenes.narration: The same kind of areas that react to food or money.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character smiles dreamily at a plate of pizza.

scenes.narration: So here's how it sneaks in.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character listens to a friend who looks tired after a long day at work.

scenes.narration: One sociologist called it the shift response.
scenes.image_prompt: A railway switch turning a train onto a different track, evening light.
scenes.fact_source: Derber, C. (1979; 2000). The Pursuit of Attention: Power and Ego in Everyday Life. Oxford University Press

scenes.narration: Your friend says, I'm so tired this week.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character's friend slumps on a sofa with dark circles under her eyes.

scenes.narration: And you say, oh, me too, let me tell you about mine.
scenes.image_prompt: A spotlight sliding from one chair to another on an empty stage.
scenes.fact_source: Derber, C. (1979; 2000). The Pursuit of Attention: Power and Ego in Everyday Life. Oxford University Press

scenes.narration: You meant to connect. But you took the spotlight.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character realises his mistake, hand over his mouth, wincing.

scenes.narration: The other option is the support response.
scenes.image_prompt: A strong wooden bridge over a calm river at sunrise.
scenes.fact_source: Derber, C. (1979; 2000). The Pursuit of Attention: Power and Ego in Everyday Life. Oxford University Press

scenes.narration: Tired how? What happened?

scenes.narration: One small question keeps the spotlight on them.

scenes.fact_source: Derber, C. (1979; 2000). The Pursuit of Attention: Power and Ego in Everyday Life. Oxford University Press

scenes.narration: I do this all the time, by the way.

scenes.narration: The shift response usually comes from wanting to relate, not from being selfish.
scenes.image_prompt: Two coffee cups touching on a cafe table, steam rising, soft morning light.
scenes.fact_source: Derber, C. (1979; 2000). The Pursuit of Attention: Power and Ego in Everyday Life. Oxford University Press

scenes.narration: But the other person doesn't feel related to. They feel interrupted.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character's friend looks down at her cup, quietly giving up her story.

scenes.narration: Their story gets cut off, and they rarely finish it later.
scenes.image_prompt: A half-finished drawing on a sketchpad left on a park bench, a pencil beside it.
scenes.fact_source: Derber, C. (1979; 2000). The Pursuit of Attention: Power and Ego in Everyday Life. Oxford University Press

scenes.narration: You'll still get your turn. Just not right away.

scenes.narration: And their story often gets better when you let it run.
scenes.image_prompt: A long winding path through a green valley opening to a beautiful view.
scenes.fact_source: Derber, C. (1979; 2000). The Pursuit of Attention: Power and Ego in Everyday Life. Oxford University Press

scenes.narration: Mistake two: you explain, they nod, they're lost.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character explains something at a whiteboard while two coworkers nod blankly.

scenes.narration: That's the curse of knowledge.

scenes.narration: It's why directions like 'turn by the old bakery' fail.

scenes.narration: The fix? Give one concrete example.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character draws a simple picture on a napkin for a friend in a cafe.

scenes.narration: And ask, which part should I explain better?

scenes.narration: Not 'did you understand?' Everyone says yes to that.

scenes.narration: Mistake three happens inside your head.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character nods at a friend while gears spin above his head.

scenes.narration: Researchers recorded conversations in ten languages around the world.
scenes.image_prompt: A world map on a desk with small glowing dots on different continents.

scenes.narration: From big cities to small villages.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character video-calls friends in different countries on his laptop.

scenes.narration: Everywhere, people avoided talking over each other.

scenes.narration: And the silence between turns was usually tiny.

scenes.fact_source: Stivers et al. (2009). Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation. PNAS 106, 10587-10592

scenes.narration: That's faster than you could plan a sentence from scratch.

scenes.narration: That's normal. But it has a cost.

scenes.narration: The more we rehearse, the less we hear.

scenes.narration: Ever answered a question nobody actually asked?

scenes.narration: It happens when we answer the words we expected, not the words we heard.

scenes.narration: Try this. Let them finish. Then take one breath.

scenes.narration: Then say back what you heard, in a few words.

scenes.narration: It feels slow. To them, it feels like respect.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character's friend smiles, surprised and grateful.

scenes.narration: Being understood is something people remember.
scenes.image_prompt: A handshake between two people in warm evening light on a rooftop.
scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: Quick pause. If you're enjoying this, subscribe and stay with me. We'll keep exploring how people really work, together, one question at a time. It's free, it takes one second, and it helps more curious people find us.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character smiles warmly at the viewer, waving him closer, in his cosy lamp-lit apartment.

scenes.narration: Now, the question that makes people like you.

scenes.fact_source: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. JPSP 113, 430-452

scenes.narration: Mistake four: you don't ask enough.

scenes.narration: There it is. The open loop from the start.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character points at the viewer with a big grin.

scenes.narration: A follow-up builds on what the person just said.

scenes.narration: They say, I just got back from Italy.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character's friend shows holiday photos on a phone at a cafe.

scenes.narration: A switch is, cool, where else have you been?
scenes.image_prompt: A train switching tracks away from a sunny station.
scenes.fact_source: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. JPSP 113, 430-452

scenes.fact_source: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. JPSP 113, 430-452

scenes.narration: Follow-ups say, I heard you, tell me more.

scenes.fact_source: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. JPSP 113, 430-452

scenes.narration: And they're easy. You don't need clever questions.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character shrugs with a relaxed smile, hands open.

scenes.narration: Just pick one detail they said and ask about it.

scenes.image_prompt: A tidy lab room with two empty chairs and a timer on a table.
scenes.fact_source: Kardas, Kumar & Epley (2022). Overly shallow? Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation. JPSP 122, 367-398

scenes.narration: Mistake five is about the ending.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands at a door, half in and half out, awkwardly smiling.

scenes.narration: Researchers studied over nine hundred conversations.
scenes.image_prompt: A wall of small photos showing many pairs of people talking in different places.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: Each person said when they'd secretly wanted to stop.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character glances at his watch during a long chat, trying to be polite.

scenes.narration: Conversations almost never ended when both people wanted.
scenes.image_prompt: An hourglass on a cafe table with sand still running, two chairs pulled back.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: Sometimes one person wanted to leave early.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character inches toward the exit while his friend keeps talking happily.

scenes.narration: And sometimes one wished it had gone on longer.
scenes.image_prompt: A train pulling away from a platform while someone waves, golden evening.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: On average, the gap was about half the conversation.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds his hands apart, measuring, amazed.

scenes.narration: And people were bad at guessing what the other one wanted.
scenes.image_prompt: Two people walking in opposite directions on a foggy bridge at dusk.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: We're all being polite. Both of us. Silently.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character and a friend both smile stiffly at each other, both checking the time.

scenes.narration: Most of these chats were between people who'd known each other for years.
scenes.image_prompt: Old friends at a kitchen table with tea and an old photo album, soft lamp.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: The fix is kind and simple. End it on a high.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character laughs with a friend, then stands up, still smiling.

scenes.narration: Leaving while it's good is not rude.
scenes.image_prompt: A sunset over the sea at its brightest moment, warm orange sky.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: Say, I loved this, let's do it again soon.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character hugs his friend goodbye at a station, both smiling.

scenes.narration: People who wanted more still enjoyed it just as much.
scenes.image_prompt: Two coffee cups left with a little coffee still inside, sunlight on the table.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: Waiting for the other person to end it rarely works.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character and his friend stand at a door, both waiting for the other to say goodbye, laughing awkwardly.

scenes.narration: The researchers found people couldn't read when their partner wanted to stop.
scenes.image_prompt: Two people at a crossroads at dusk, each glancing at the other, street lamps flickering on.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: So someone has to be brave and kind about it.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character gently taps his friend's shoulder and smiles, ready to leave.

scenes.narration: A warm, clear goodbye is better than a slow fade.
scenes.image_prompt: A sunset fading over a calm lake, the last light on the water.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: And the next chat starts warmer.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character receives a smiling message notification on his phone at home.

scenes.narration: A good ending makes people want to come back.
scenes.image_prompt: A front door with a welcome mat, light glowing inside, autumn leaves on the steps.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: So let's put it together.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits at a desk with a fresh notebook under a warm lamp at night.

scenes.narration: One. People probably like you more than you think.
scenes.image_prompt: Two friends laughing on a city rooftop at sunset.
scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: Stop grading yourself. Watch them instead.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character puts down an imaginary scorecard and looks up, relaxed.

scenes.narration: Two. When they share, stay on their story.
scenes.image_prompt: A single warm spotlight on one armchair in a quiet room.
scenes.fact_source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29, 1742-1756

scenes.narration: Ask, what happened next?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character nods along as a friend talks excitedly.

scenes.narration: Three. Give an example, and ask what to explain better.
scenes.image_prompt: A napkin drawing on a cafe table with a pencil beside it.
scenes.fact_source: Newton, E. (1990). Stanford PhD dissertation (song-tapping study); described in Heath & Heath (2007), Made to Stick

scenes.narration: Four. Finish listening before you plan.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character takes a calm breath while his friend talks at a bus stop, rain falling.

scenes.narration: One breath. Then say back what you heard.
scenes.image_prompt: Ripples spreading slowly across a calm pond at dawn.
scenes.fact_source: Stivers et al. (2009). Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation. PNAS 106, 10587-10592

scenes.narration: Five. Ask one follow-up. Maybe a deep one.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character leans in with real curiosity across a dinner table.

scenes.narration: Follow-ups were the strongest link to liking in the study.
scenes.image_prompt: Stepping stones crossing a stream into a sunny meadow.
scenes.fact_source: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. JPSP 113, 430-452

scenes.narration: And end while it's still good.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves goodbye with a big smile outside a cafe at dusk.

scenes.narration: Almost no conversation ends at the perfect moment anyway.
scenes.image_prompt: An hourglass with the last grains of sand falling, warm light.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: You don't need to be charming. Just curious.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character smiles at the viewer, hands in his pockets, sunny street.

scenes.narration: Curiosity looks the same in every language.
scenes.image_prompt: People in different countries chatting in markets and cafes, bright morning light.
scenes.fact_source: Stivers et al. (2009). Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation. PNAS 106, 10587-10592

scenes.narration: Here's my honest take. Nobody is perfect at this.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character laughs at himself, covering his face after an awkward joke.

scenes.narration: Even the people who study conversation still have awkward ones.
scenes.image_prompt: A conference hall coffee break where people chat in small clumsy groups.
scenes.fact_source: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney & Wilson (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS 118, e2011809118

scenes.narration: Try just one thing this week.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character writes one small note and sticks it on his fridge.

scenes.narration: Small changes in how we listen can change how people feel around us.
scenes.image_prompt: A circle of friends around a table, everyone leaning in, warm string lights.
scenes.fact_source: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. JPSP 113, 430-452

scenes.narration: Thank you for spending these minutes with me. If this helped, hit like, and tell me in the comments which mistake you catch yourself making. I read every one. Next time, we'll find out why saying no feels so hard. See you there, friend.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves goodbye from his sunny balcony, a coffee cup in hand and city rooftops behind him.
